demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: There is something about me that made the event happen
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

vignette:
Graham, a 54-year-old forester, still feels the weight of the chainsaw in his hands. Three years ago, on a clear October afternoon, he was felling a marked oak on a ridge above a hiking trail. He had checked his drop zone twice, but a sudden gust of wind twisted the crown, and the tree swung off its intended path. He heard the scream before he saw the man—a hiker who had wandered off the marked path, now pinned beneath the trunk. Graham ran down the slope, screaming for help on his radio, but by the time the medics arrived, the man’s leg was crushed beyond saving. In the weeks that followed, Graham could not stop replaying the moment the tree began to fall—not just the image, but the sensation of his own arms holding the saw, the vibration in his palms, the exact angle of his stance. When the memory surfaced, his body would lock into that same posture: shoulders braced, hands gripping an invisible handle, heart pounding as if the saw were still running. What frightened him most was the rage that followed, a white-hot fury at the hiker for being there, at the wind, at himself—rage that felt as fresh as the day it happened, and that left him ashamed and hollow.

The physical pain in his lower back, where he had strained himself running down the hill, became a trigger he could not escape. Every time he bent to lift a log or climbed into his truck, the ache would flare, and the thought would come unbidden: *This is because of what I did.* He had come to believe that there was something fundamentally wrong with him—some intrinsic fault that had caused the accident, some hidden carelessness he could not see but others could. He told his wife, Marie, that he could no longer trust himself to make even simple decisions. "I can't rely on myself anymore," he said one night, staring at the kitchen floor. He stopped volunteering for the fire crew, stopped leading trail maintenance. He felt he was no longer capable of the work that had defined him for thirty years.

Graham began watching other people closely. On the rare occasions he drove into town, he scanned every stranger's face for signs of accusation. When a man at the hardware store held his gaze a moment too long, Graham felt his chest tighten—he was certain the man knew, that everyone in the county knew what he had done. He found he could not relax, even at home in his own living room. He sat with his back to the wall, facing the door, listening for footsteps. The threat felt constant, though he knew logically that no one was coming. This vigilance, in turn, made the memories more vivid. The more he scanned for danger, the more his mind threw him back to the moment of impact—the sound, the angle of the sun, the way the saw's chain had been slick with sap. And each memory reinforced his belief that he was a danger to others, that he could not be trusted in the world.

His work suffered. He began avoiding the western section of the forest entirely, where the accident had occurred, and took longer routes to avoid any trailhead where hikers might be present. Physical proximity to other people, especially strangers on the logging roads, sent his heart racing. He stopped eating lunch in the communal break room, preferring to sit alone in his truck. His supervisor noticed and asked if something was wrong. Graham said he was fine, but he knew he was not. The grief would hit him without warning—not just for the hiker, whose name he had learned was Daniel, but for the life he had lost, for the person he used to be. He had come to believe that the accident had revealed a truth about himself he had never seen before, and that truth could not be undone.

What finally brought Graham to seek help was a morning in late March, when he found himself standing in the middle of a clear-cut, unable to remember how he had gotten there, his hands shaking, his body locked in the posture of the fall. He called a therapist the same afternoon. What he was most afraid of was that she would confirm what he already suspected—that he was broken in a way that could not be fixed. But he was also, quietly, hoping that she might tell him otherwise.
